title: A High-Fidelity Cardiac Digital Twin for Assessing Rate-Dependent Responses: A Comparative Multi-scale Study of TT2 and Tomek Models in Stratified 3D Ventricles
comment: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention -- MICCAI 2026 Workshops and Challenges
summary: Cardiac digital twins (CDTs) provide a computational platform for personalized cardiac modeling, but their predictive behavior depends strongly on the selected ionic model and the representation of transmural electrophysiological heterogeneity. In this study, we developed a multiscale CDT validation framework that integrates physiologically optimized hierarchical configurations. Using single-cell (0D) models and three-dimensional (3D) patient-specific ventricular models, we implemented the ten Tusscher-Panfilov model (TT2) and Tomek ionic model and compared their electrophysiological responses across a range of pacing frequencies, with basic cycle lengths (BCLs) from 600 to 4000 ms. The results show that tissue-level electrical coupling substantially reshapes the intrinsic dynamical properties observed at the single-cell level. By benchmarking model outputs against clinical data, this study quantifies fidelity differences between the two ionic models across multiple scales and provides a scientific basis for ionic model selection and CDT construction.

title: A novel model-based equation for size dependent mean recovery coefficients for spheres and other shapes
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures, 1 table, 3 appendices
summary: Background: In NM-imaging, theoretical curves for the recovery coefficient (RC) of the signal maximum and mean are known for spheres and cubes, if a 3D Gaussian PSF is assumed. The RC of the maximum is also known for cylinders. For these and other shapes empirical equations with one or two fit-parameters have been utilized. Methods: An equation for the RC for large objects of arbitrary shape is derived and generalized into an empirical equation for smaller objects, which is verified by numerical simulations. The proposed equation is compared to published results on SPECT kidney phantom measurements and to PET measurements on the NEMA IEC PET body phantom with six spheres. Results: The signal loss (1-RC) for large spheres is inversely proportional to the radius, where the slope is proportional to the FWHM of the spatial resolution. For non-spherical shapes the generalized instead of the volume equivalent radius should be utilized. For smaller objects, an equation with one added empirical fit-parameter is presented. It is demonstrated that the EANM-guidelines' two-parameter logistic function results in a poor fit if the theoretical slope and inverse proportionality are forced and it gives a suboptimal fit when both parameters are fitted. Conclusions: A novel model-based equation for the mean RC-curve is derived. It can be used for arbitrary shapes as long as the sphericity is taken into account and it is accurate down to RC=10%. One parameter is directly related to the spatial resolution, while the other is a shape depending fit-parameter.

title: EQUIP-RPT: A framework for objective evaluation of quantitative imaging methods in radiopharmaceutical therapies
comment: 33 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in the Journal of Medical Imaging
summary:
Quantitative imaging (QI) provides a non-invasive approach for dosimetry and quantitative response assessment in radiopharmaceutical therapies (RPTs). QI methods are being developed for instrumentation, acquisition, reconstruction, and image analysis. However, a key barrier to routine adoption of these methods is that evidence demonstrating reliable performance of QI methods on clinically relevant quantification tasks in RPTs remains limited. Our goal is to outline the Evaluation of Quantitative Imaging Performance in Radiopharmaceutical Therapy (EQUIP-RPT) framework, a structured approach for objective, task-based evaluation of QI methods for RPTs.
  We outline the EQUIP-RPT framework based on image-science and task-based image-quality evaluation methodology, practical considerations, and recent literature. The framework is organized around four linked design steps: (i) specification of the quantification task, (ii) design of the study population and imaging protocol, (iii) task-specific information extraction, and (iv) selection of figures of merit (FoMs).
  The EQUIP-RPT framework is presented in the context of four quantification tasks in RPT: activity uptake, absorbed dose, volumetric tumor burden, and lesion-level longitudinal quantifications. The framework distinguishes two paradigms for task-specific information extraction and organizes FoMs according to the performance attributes they characterize. We describe key elements to apply the EQUIP-RPT framework in simulation, physical phantom, and clinical studies. Finally, we show how EQUIP-RPT can be used to generate a quantitative claim based on the evaluation study.
  The EQUIP-RPT framework is designed to provide a structured approach for objective task-based evaluation of QI methods in RPTs, thereby facilitating clinical translation of these methods.

title: Subwavelength registration of skull-compensating acoustic holograms via nonlinear parametric array feedback
comment: 25 pages, 13 figures (6 main, 7 supplementary), 2 tables. Adapted from the first author's Ph.D. dissertation at the Georgia Institute of Technology (2026)
summary: Realizing the potential of optimized acoustic holograms for applications like transcranial ultrasound requires sub-wavelength alignment accuracy (less than 1.5 mm at 1 MHz), which is difficult to achieve with current non-MRI optical neuro-navigation methods. To address the critical challenge of alignment, we leverage the parametric array (PA) signal as an alignment surrogate, a highly penetrative, low-frequency difference wave generated by the nonlinear mixing of two primary high-frequency beams. Simulations show that a misaligned skull-compensating lens increases the primary acoustic energy within the skull bone (volumetric energy trapping), which strengthens the nonlinear source of the PA signal. We also tested whether shear-mode conversion in bone contributes: 2D elastic simulations showed only a small (3-5%) increase in shear-type motion with misalignment, and the transmitted ex vivo bursts did not lengthen as a shear path would require. Pseudo-sound and microbubble artifacts were examined and found unlikely to explain the signal, consistent with the PA signal arising from the intrinsic nonlinearity of the bone. Minimizing this PA signal yields a noninvasive real-time feedback mechanism that achieves sub-wavelength alignment accuracy, outperforming standard neuronavigation. Our findings present a robust framework that supports the design of simple, economical, and high-performance transcranial ultrasound systems for high-precision neuro-interventions.

title: Stretched bilayer-cytoskeleton links hold echinocytes in a model splenic slit
comment: 35 pages, 8 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Materials included (pages S1-S16, 6 figures, 1 table); Movies S1 to S3 are ancillary files. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Stored red blood cells become echinocytes, growing spicules before losing membrane; the spleen clears the resulting small, spherical cells. Whether spicules alone hinder splenic passage is unknown. Shape and area change together. In a two-component model whose shrinking cytoskeleton raises spicules, we drove a discocyte and stage I to III echinocytes of equal area and volume through a model splenic slit. The pressure drop needed to pass rose with stage; stage III echinocytes were held at 37 to 50 times the pressure drop that passed the discocyte. Bilayer-cytoskeleton links stretched near full extension held these cells; lengthening them about twofold released a held cell. Capillary-sized channels, as in our device, separated the stages far less. Of the shape classes in stored blood, the model held at high pressure drops only storage-induced microerythrocytes, which perfused human spleens clear most. Spicules, besides membrane loss, may decide which stored cells the spleen retains.

title: Selecting Person Segmentation Models for Real-Time Video Call Backgrounds on the CPU
summary: Background blur and background replacement are now normal parts of a video call. Many open models and open source pipelines can do this, but it is hard to know which one to pick. Speed, edge quality and license all matter, and they are often reported on different hardware, or not reported at all. In this work we ran 20 setups on the same laptop CPU, with the same 640x480 frames and the same output view. The setups are 15 open models and 5 complete open source pipelines. We measured frames per second on a test clip and on a live webcam, compared the masks on a public domain portrait and on three video call photos with a raised hand, one of them a close front camera view, and recorded the license of every model. The fastest setups reach more than 40 frames per second on a laptop CPU, while the slowest, a high detail model for still images, needs several seconds per frame. A few setups give clean edges and still run in real time. We also found that the runtime library and the steps around the model can change the speed by several times. Based on these results we give a guide that tells the reader which model to choose for a given need, such as a weak laptop, the best hair edges, a closed source product, or people behind the speaker.

title: Silscore: modelling siRNA potency with positional thermodynamics and data-selected nucleotide-identity terms
comment: 25 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) enable programmable gene silencing, but candidates targeting the same transcript can differ markedly in potency. Existing predictors range from interpretable empirical rules with limited accuracy to high-capacity models that can lose performance when datasets or targets change. We present Silscore, a guide-only model that combines a quadratic preference for overall duplex stability, a position-resolved profile of nearest-neighbour stacking energies and sparse nucleotide-identity terms selected from residuals left unexplained by thermodynamics. Its main fit uses 26 parameters, fewer than half as many as any trainable comparator evaluated here. We evaluate Silscore on the canonical split of the Huesken dataset, two external datasets (Mixset and Katoh-Suzuki), and an evaluation in which the same guides are tested after training on dissimilar targets. Silscore attains the highest observed Pearson correlation in all three transfer evaluations, and the data support an advantage over every applicable comparator on Katoh-Suzuki. For a fixed evaluation set, we compare two equally sized training sets with higher or lower sequence similarity to the evaluation sequences. After training on the less similar sequences, Silscore has the highest observed correlation, and the data do not establish a change in its performance. The fitted parameters can also be interpreted directly: identity terms locate sequence effects that base-pairing energies cannot express, global stability has a data-estimated intermediate optimum, and local energy profiles recover terminal asymmetry and a preference for weaker seed and stronger central pairing. Silscore thus provides a compact, data-driven model that combines strong predictive performance with robustness when tested in new settings and expresses previously reported empirical preferences as quantities estimated from data.

title: Spontaneous mechanical patterning in active elastic tissues with stress feedback
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, SI appended
summary: The active mechanics of biological tissues is often governed by embedded active contractile fibers responding to mechanical feedback. We introduce a minimal model of a solid-like tissue where the mechanics is controlled by feedback of local active and elastic stresses on fiber organization. The resulting tissue generically exhibits a bistable response to external strain and spontaneously segregates into domains of orthogonally aligned fibers. Our theory thus provides a minimal mechanical feedback mechanism generating orthogonal structural alignment ubiquitous in biological tissues.

title: Improving Airflow Network Models of Natural Ventilation: Geometry-Specific Pressures and Fluctuation Corrections
comment: 30 pages, 11 figures
summary: Building energy models typically predict natural ventilation rates using airflow networks, which solve a system of orifice equations with exterior pressures as boundary conditions. This study investigates two improvements to these models: (i) geometry-specific exterior pressures obtained from large eddy simulations (LESs) and (ii) analytical corrections accounting for the nonlinear effects of pressure fluctuations on mean ventilation rates. We evaluate these improvements against coupled interior-exterior LESs of flows through 5824 windows, 2688 skylights, and 2752 interiors across idealized urban canopies. Replacing standard ASHRAE pressure coefficients with pressures from exterior-only LESs reduces the RMSE of predicted ventilation rates by approximately 50%, largely by capturing urban canopy flow effects that are poorly represented by standard shelter factors. Independently of the pressure source, mean-pressure airflow network predictions exhibit a nonlinear relationship with the LES ventilation rates. To address this discrepancy, we derive fluctuation corrections for mean-dominated and fluctuation-dominated flow regimes. These corrections eliminate the systematic nonlinearity and further reduce RMSE by 10-40% for most opening types and ventilation configurations. For windows, the combined improvements from geometry-specific surface pressures and fluctuation corrections increase the coefficient of determination $R^2$ from approximately 0.4 to 0.9. The results demonstrate the potential to accurately predict natural ventilation rates across different interior layouts while accounting for urban canopy effects and pressure fluctuations, using exterior-only LES pressure information.

title: A Low-Cost MR-Compatible Pneumatic Motion Phantom for Magnetic Resonance Imaging
comment: 22 pages with references
summary: We describe the detailed design, construction, and testing of a simple, low-cost, open-source, exclusively pneumatic phantom for gated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies of cyclic motion. The overall phantom cost is approximately $200. It is designed to use widely-available materials and an easy-to-program, adaptable micro-controller. Image contrast is generated with air pumped through mineral oil. We demonstrate the utility of the phantom for simulating simple organ motion when developing and investigating image acquisition and reconstruction methods. Phantom motion was independently characterized by video analysis and found to be highly repeatable, with a cycle-to-cycle period variation of 0.6% and a stroke volume variation of 2.3%. The phantom does not generate electromagnetic interference, making it a suitable option for unshielded ultra-low field (ULF) MRI systems. To our knowledge, this work reports the first motion phantom to be imaged on an ULF MRI system

title: One Block Is Enough: LoopMR for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Code: https://github.com/hym97/LoopMR
summary: Deep-learning unrolled networks are the leading approach to accelerated MRI reconstruction. State-of-the-art models such as PromptMR+ learn a distinct block for every cascade, so their size grows with the number of cascades. Sharing one block across iterations avoids adding parameters, but earlier shared-weight models typically used a tiny block and produced worse images than models with distinct weights. Therefore, it remained unclear whether weight sharing itself or the choice of block was the problem. Recent advances in looped transformers, which reuse the same block across layers, show that they can match or outperform their distinct-weight counterparts on several tasks. Motivated by this, we propose LoopMR, which reuses a single Restormer block at every iteration as its core. Besides the current image estimate, the block receives data-consistency inputs and latent images. On four datasets covering the brain (CC359), knee (fastMRI), heart (CMRxRecon2023) and carotid (in-house), LoopMR significantly outperforms E2E-VarNet, PromptMR and PromptMR+ in PSNR and SSIM at every acceleration factor (p < 0.01), with about 1/9 of PromptMR+'s parameters (10.3M versus 92.9M). It also keeps its lead at unseen acceleration factors and on an unseen dataset. With our transformer block, the shared model matches or outperforms its distinct-weight counterpart at 6, 12 and 24 iterations. At a fixed number of iterations, shared transformer blocks match or outperform their distinct-weight versions, while shared CNN blocks perform worse. These results suggest that looping one well-chosen block can outperform stacking distinct cascades in MRI reconstruction, with a fraction of the parameters.

title: CupOFMoCA: Coupled Objective-Guided Discrete Flows for Molecular Conjugate Assembly
comment: Published at NeurIPS 2026. (Proceedings of the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, Sydney, Australia)
summary: Molecular conjugates, including PROTACs and peptide-drug conjugates (PDCs), derive their function from the joint behavior of multiple coupled components, yet most generative approaches design these components independently and combine them only after generation. Such staged pipelines ignore cross-component dependencies and often produce conjugates that are chemically invalid, fall outside empirical conjugate distributions, or lose function upon assembly. In this work, we introduce Coupled Objective-Guided Discrete Flows for Molecular Conjugate Assembly (CupOFMoCA), a discrete generative method that enforces cross-component chemical constraints during conjugate generation. CupOFMoCA restricts guided updates to chemically feasible conjugate states and reweights local transitions using molecular design objectives. Across three PDC systems, coupled generation achieved 100% conjugation validity among valid peptides and increased valid yield over matched post-hoc filtering, with comparable predicted binding scores across the full valid sets. In three-seed evaluations of three PROTAC systems, CupOFMoCA achieved the highest assembly validity on two systems and generated more assembly-valid molecules per second than the evaluated baselines. We further evaluated the generated PROTACs with post-hoc DegradeMaster scoring and explicit-solvent molecular dynamics, supporting their predicted activity and conformational properties. Together, these results establish CupOFMoCA as an efficient generator of molecular conjugates, supporting therapeutic development via coordinated control of assembly and molecular properties.

title: Feedback-induced mechanical bistability and perpendicular-domain formation in active elastic tissues
comment: 23 pages, 12 figures, 1 Appendix
summary: Contractile fibers in muscle tissues are highly aligned over the scale of many cells. Muscle layers surrounding organs with an inner lumen are often arranged in orthogonal directions. Here, we study a minimal mechanism of how structural order and its patterning into orthogonally aligned domains can emerge from mechanical feedback alone. The central idea is that contractile fibers align in the direction of the local active and elastic stresses, a feedback motivated by the maturation of muscle fibers under tension. We thus model muscle tissue as an active nematic solid with stress feedback: an elastic medium with embedded contractile fibers that are reinforced along the directions of the local tissue stresses. We find that the feedback from the contractile fiber stress is self-amplifying and drives spontaneous fiber alignment. Feedback from the elastic stress couples the alignment to the mechanical boundary conditions and tissue geometry. Depending on the mechanical boundary conditions, the elastic-stress feedback stabilizes two orthogonally aligned tissue states, resulting in a structurally and mechanically bistable tissue that shows a hysteretic stress-strain response. In spatially extended tissues, this bistability gives rise to orthogonally aligned domains separated by domain walls. In an annulus surrounding a pressurized lumen, a radially aligned inner domain and a circumferentially aligned outer domain stably coexist because the domain wall is pinned at a position that results in the fibers carrying the lumen pressure. Our results show that stress feedback can pattern structural order by coupling spontaneous alignment to the tissue geometry. Our mechanism thus provides a purely mechanical route to orthogonal fiber patterning in muscle tissues.

title: Comparison of the flamelet progress variable and thickened flame models for LES of turbulent combustion
comment: 14 Pages, 15 Figures, To be submitted to Combustion and Flame
summary: Large-eddy simulation (LES) of turbulent combustion requires closure models for unresolved flame structures and chemical processes. Two widely used but fundamentally different approaches are the flamelet/progress-variable approach (FPVA) and the dynamically thickened-flame model (TFM). Here, both are applied to methane-air combustion within a common numerical framework and evaluated for the Sandia D flame and a jet-in-crossflow representative of a non-assist waste-gas flare across a range of crosswind-to-jet velocity ratios. For the predominantly diffusion-controlled Sandia-D flame, FPVA and TFM exhibit similar accuracy, while FPVA is substantially less computationally expensive and converges faster under mesh refinement. More detailed chemical kinetics improve agreement with experimental measurements, with little additional cost for FPVA but a substantial increase for TFM. For the jet-in-crossflow, both approaches reproduce the experimentally observed reduction in combustion efficiency with increasing crosswind, but their predictions progressively diverge as the crosswind strength increases. This divergence coincides with the emergence of a locally premixed reaction branch captured by TFM but not represented by FPVA, whereas predictions in diffusion-dominated regions remain broadly similar. In TFM, the locally premixed branch is associated with elevated scalar dissipation and greater residual methane downstream, indicating that highly strained premixed combustion contributes to differences in predicted flare performance. These results show that FPVA and TFM can provide similar predictions in diffusion-dominated flames but differ substantially when crossflow induces locally premixed, highly strained combustion near the nozzle.

title: Multi-UTE Myelin Fraction Mapping: Repeatability and Cross-Field-Strength Reproducibility at 1.5T and 3T
comment: 7 Figures, 2 Tables, 7 Supplementary Figures
summary: Purpose: To evaluate the repeatability and cross-field-strength reproducibility (1.5T vs 3T) of in vivo cerebral myelin fraction (MF) mapping with multi-contrast dual-resolution 3D UTE (multi-UTE), and to compare it with magnetization transfer (MT)-based methods. Methods: MT methods provide an indirect myelin-sensitive measure derived from magnetization exchange between macromolecular and free-water proton pools, whereas multi-UTE targets the ultrashort-T2* signal components. In five healthy volunteers, multi-UTE and MT-based measurements were performed at 1.5T and 3T, and the calculated MF maps were compared with magnetization transfer ratio (MTR) and magnetization transfer saturation (MTsat) maps. Two volunteers underwent repeated multi-UTE measurements within and between days. Field-strength reproducibility and test-retest repeatability were evaluated using linear regression, Bland-Altman analysis, concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Results: Multi-UTE enabled simultaneous acquisition of quantitative and high-resolution structural images at both 1.5T and 3T. MF repeatability was high at 3T (ICC = 0.94-0.96) and more variable at 1.5T (0,64-0.96). Across field strengths, MF and MTsat showed comparable reproducibility (CCC 0.70 vs 0.60) with small median absolute differences (8.8% vs 8.9%). MTsat showed tighter correlation (R2 = 0.77 vs 0.68), while MF showed a wider inter-regional dynamic range. MTR differed strongly between field strengths (CCC = 0.06). Conclusion: Multi-UTE MF, obtained without B1 or T1 mapping and alongside a high-resolution structural image, achieves cross-field reproducibility comparable to, but not exceeding, MTsat. Lower SNR at 1.5T and unmodelled T1 weighting may have contributed to residual field dependence.

title: Aggregate Accuracy Hides Diagnosis-Specific Failure in Medical Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Medical Reasoning with Vision Language Foundation Models (Med-Reasoner). 16 pages including NeurIPS checklist, 1 figure, 5 tables
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) are compared mainly by accuracy averaged across findings, a summary that can hide complete failure on a single diagnosis. We audit five open medical VLMs (MedGemma-4B, Lingshu-7B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and MedVLM-R1) on 6,048 ChestX-ray14 questions balanced by sex, age, finding, and label. On the 432 pneumothorax-positive X-rays, HuatuoGPT-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL detect zero cases while MedGemma and Lingshu detect 38% and 67% of the same images. The two failing models answer "no" to all 864 pneumothorax cases (balanced accuracy 0.500, chance), yet produce fluent, anatomically specific explanations that name the signs of a collapsed lung and then deny them, with no hedge or abstention. This failure is not an artifact of prompting, image resolution, label ambiguity, or model scale. It persists across four prompt formats, at native resolution, and on single-label cases. A within-model control shows the same forced prompt gives HuatuoGPT 79% recall on nodule but only 6% on pneumothorax. It survives a tenfold scale increase (Qwen2.5-VL-72B detects 4%) and replicates on SIIM-ACR, an independent dataset with radiologist-drawn masks, where the failing models detect 0 of 432 confirmed pneumothoraces, including 0 of the 144 largest lesions. Reading the models' logits and internal states shows this is not blindness. The two failing models are highly confident yet no better than chance and a linear probe recovers pneumothorax from their hidden representations even where recall is zero, so the finding is represented internally but suppressed at the output. Aggregate accuracy therefore cannot establish that a medical VLM can see a given finding, because a model that misses one can still describe it convincingly. Reporting per-finding recall and specificity on balanced cases is needed to tell the difference.

title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
comment: To be published on Annual Review Biomedical Data Science
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models' outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.

title: A unified finite-site framework for scaffold-client biocondensation
summary: Client recruitment into biomolecular condensates does not determine how stronger binding changes the bulk free-energy advantage of demixing. Here, we use a unified finite-site thermodynamic framework to examine how scaffold-client interactions affect both the response of a fixed-composition mixture and the organization of its ternary phase diagram. The thermodynamic response to increasing client affinity is determined by the difference in heterotypic bonding between the complete equilibrium phase-separated sample and the corresponding homogeneous state. A finite region of the model exhibits positive scaffold-client concentration covariance but negative heterotypic bond contrast: stronger binding reduces the demixing advantage even when both species enrich in the dense phase. This reduction also occurs with independent scaffold self-association and client-binding site pools, without direct displacement of scaffold bonds. A negative response does not by itself imply condensate shrinkage or dissolution. Across composition space, the same finite binding constraints support scaffold-rich and heterotypic coexistence regimes with distinct bond populations. For divalent clients, these regimes can occupy disconnected regions of the phase diagram and reconnect upon increasing client affinity, depending on scaffold cohesion. Critical-point continuation identifies the folds and cusp organizing these changes, while client valence restricts the parameter range over which disconnected coexistence occurs. Explicit-particle Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the qualitative reentrant response and provide finite-size evidence for disconnected coexistence. These results provide a bond-resolved characterization of fixed-parent affinity response and a complementary description of coexistence under specified association constraints.

title: Harmonic structure and parametric prediction of instantaneous power in oscillating foils
comment: 29 pages, 15 figures, submitted to Journal of Fluid Mechanics
summary: A closed-form model is developed to predict the instantaneous lift, pitching moment, and power of an oscillating-foil energy harvester directly from its kinematic input. Such foils extract renewable power from moving water through sinusoidal heaving and pitching. However, due to their large-amplitude motion and vortex-dominated dynamics, classical unsteady aerodynamics cannot accurately predict the time-dependent force and power generation. To generate the model, 405 two-dimensional simulations are computed which vary heave amplitude, pitch amplitude, and frequency, representing the energy harvesting kinematic parameter space. The lift and pitching moment are decomposed into odd Fourier harmonics, and each Fourier coefficient is regressed on sixteen physics-based polynomial terms derived from the kinematic, power, and energy scalings. The regression is performed in two Ridge steps, one for attribution and one for the deployable predictor. The attribution shows that the first harmonic, which contains the mean power, depends on the motion amplitudes. The higher harmonics respond nonlinearly to the frequency, which determines the number and timing of the vortex shedding. The model recovers the cycle-averaged power with a leave-one-out $R^2$ of $0.98$, and reproduces the instantaneous lift with a median peak error of $9\%$ and a median phase error below $1\%$ of the period. The harmonic order of the response counts the discrete vortex events in each stroke, as confirmed by the wake visualization. The model's analytical expression for time-dependent force and power can be utilized as a fast and accurate alternative to high-fidelity simulations, specifically targeting device design and array optimization of oscillating foils.

title: A Feasibility Study of Whole-Cerebrum Task-Based fMRI at 0.55 T: Motor and Visual Tasks Using Single-Shot EPI
summary: Purpose: To evaluate the feasibility of whole-cerebrum task-based fMRI on a modern 0.55T system, examining the effects of extended scan duration and within-session consistency on functional mapping outcomes and comparison to acquisition with matched tasks at 3.0T. Methods: Six healthy participants were scanned at 0.55T using a single-shot EPI sequence during bilateral finger-tapping and visual checkerboard tasks. Data were processed using an open-source pipeline. To investigate sensitivity improvements, two consecutive 5-minute runs were concatenated. Within-session consistency was also assessed. A representative 3T dataset provided additional reference context for temporal dynamics and statistical sensitivity. Results: Task-evoked activations were detected at 0.55T using Family-Wise Error (FWE) rate correction (p < 0.05) in both motor and visual cortices. While single 5-minute runs provided baseline detectability, extending the acquisition to 10 minutes increased t-statistic magnitudes and cluster extents while substantially reducing background noise (47% reduction in voxelwise dispersion). Run-to-run comparisons showed consistent peak locations and statistical significance across participants. Comparison with the 3T reference demonstrated that statistical significance increases with acquisition time so that a 0.55T scan approximately matches 3T significance levels at twice the scan duration across the range compared. Conclusion: Whole-cerebrum task fMRI is feasible at 0.55T using standard EPI and modern high-performance gradients. These results indicate that modest extensions in scan duration can compensate for reduced intrinsic BOLD sensitivity at lower field strengths.

title: Coarse-to-Fine 3D MRI Reconstruction via Resolution-Agnostic Neural Operators
comment: NeurIPS 2026
summary: Deep-learning-based 3D MRI reconstruction is limited in practice by the GPU memory and compute cost of full-volume training; 3D acquisitions are thus most often reconstructed by 2D models applied slice-by-slice and then stacked, which ignores through-plane (stacking-axis) structure. We reconstruct in full 3D and ask whether a model can be trained at low resolution (fast and memory-feasible) yet deployed at higher resolution. This coarse-to-fine strategy needs reliable cross-resolution performance, but standard networks are resolution-specific and degrade substantially when evaluated outside the training setting. We therefore use resolution-agnostic neural operators (NOs) and propose KIR-NO (k-space-to-Image Reconstruction Neural Operator), a discretization-agnostic framework for accelerated 3D MRI reconstruction. KIR-NO is trained with full backpropagation on low-resolution volumes and applied zero-shot to higher-resolution volumes at inference. Its core building block is a 3D neural operator based on discrete-continuous convolutions: convolutional filters are parameterized in a continuous basis and sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions while preserving the local inductive bias of convolution. KIR-NO integrates these learned operators with physics-based consistency: a k-space neural-operator head first refines the undersampled Fourier measurements, and image-space neural-operator cascades then refine the reconstruction through interleaved data-consistency updates. Across 3D knee and brain MRI benchmarks, KIR-NO improves over classical and CNN baselines: it improves over a state-of-the-art 3D CNN by 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4x acceleration on SKM-TEA, with gains persisting at 8x and 16x. These results show that resolution-agnostic operators make coarse-to-fine 3D MRI reconstruction - cheap low-resolution training with high-resolution deployment - practical across anatomies.

title: Proliferating against the current: how multistep branching nucleation can sort microtubule polarity in the spindle
summary: The spindle, which segregates chromosomes during cell division, is a paradigm of cytoskeletal self-organization: a highly ordered structure that persists for hours is assembled from dynamic microtubules that branch, grow, slide, and turn over within tens of seconds. Its microtubules point inward, with minus ends clustered at the poles and plus ends extending toward the chromosomes at the center of the structure. In large meiotic spindles this arrangement is puzzling, since microtubules nucleate near the chromosomes and grow at their plus ends much faster than motors slide them backward. One would therefore expect the plus ends, rather than the minus ends, to radiate outward. Here, we propose a resolution to this seeming paradox through a kinetic model that integrates the core filament-level processes. When branching complexes assemble with a sufficient delay, for instance through several sequential rate-limiting steps, they accumulate on old microtubule lattice sites near the backward-sliding minus ends of mother microtubules. Each generation is then born farther back than the last, so the self-renewing population drifts toward the minus ends even though each filament's center advances toward its plus end. For the sliding and growth velocities measured in Xenopus egg extract spindles, a multistep mechanism requires at least four rate-limiting steps. The kinetic theory has a surprisingly amenable structure: the filament length configuration variable can be eliminated exactly, yielding a finite space-time hierarchy, and the direction of population drift follows from a general criterion comparing the mean lattice age at branching sites with the ratio of plus-end advance to sliding speed.

title: Experimental Investigation of Hypersonic Shock-Wave/Boundary-Layer Interaction Dynamics Using Plasma-Generated Disturbances
summary: The unsteady dynamics of a transitional 3D shock-wave/boundary-layer interaction (SWBLI) are investigated using pulsed plasma disturbances on a cone-slice-ramp geometry in the Boeing/AFOSR Mach-6 Quiet Tunnel. Nanosecond-duration repetitively pulsed spark discharges introduce disturbances which convect through the interaction, causing transient turbulent breakdown in the reattaching shear layer. The unsteady behavior of the separation bubble is characterized using schlieren imaging, and natural broadband unsteadiness is observed in the form of large-scale shock and separation flapping at frequencies below 1500 Hz ($Sr_L< 0.25$). Disturbance packets are introduced at a range of perturbation frequencies and generally induce shear layer oscillations; however, perturbation frequencies below the natural cutoff frequency ($f\approx 1500$ $\mathrm{Hz}$) yield fluctuations with significantly larger amplitudes than those above this frequency. Phase-averaged schlieren images reveal that the disturbances cause a decrease in shear layer height immediately after inducing turbulent breakdown around the reattachment point, with this displacement beginning downstream and moving upstream. The shear layer's response to this displacement is consistent with that of an under-damped dynamic system with a preferred oscillation frequency; the measured frequency of the oscillatory response to external perturbation ($f = 1464$ Hz) is also the approximate cutoff frequency of the natural broadband unsteadiness. Furthermore, the relationship between perturbation frequency and oscillation amplitude resembles that of a low-pass filter, with a cutoff frequency that is within 5\% of the measured oscillator frequency. These experimental findings support the theory that the cutoff frequency for the SWBLI's frequency-selective amplification is tied to the time scale of the weakly damped global mode.

title: Interpreting Selective-Review Coverage for Head-and-Neck Auto-Contours
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
summary: Selective-review systems aim to reduce human review by passing candidates predicted to be low risk. However, coverage (the fraction passed) can be misleading when measurements needed to interpret risk are unavailable. We separate structural evaluability (a nonempty mask with all required measurements available), computational-endpoint status, and pass-or-review decisions using archived Mayo records and controlled OpenKBP analyses. In 3,968 Mayo records, all 1,167 recorded empty predictions (predicted target-organ masks containing zero voxels despite nonempty reference masks) were endpoint-negative and passed both modules, accounting for approximately 76% of each pass set. In a held-out OpenKBP test, a logistic-regression router achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.833 and average precision of 0.449 but passed all 544 non-evaluable candidates, including 542 prespecified empty-mask controls and 2 erosions that became empty. A structural gate removed those passes without changing scores or the threshold, preserved all evaluable passes, and assigned 98.71% of endpoint-positive candidates to review. Under the original preprocessing and in patient-disjoint development evaluation, a router trained only on evaluable candidates and a router modeling an unavailable state likewise passed no non-evaluable candidates, with similar evaluable discrimination and at least 99.0% of endpoint-positive candidates assigned to review in pooled outer-fold predictions. These results show that coverage should be interpreted jointly with candidate eligibility, endpoint scope, missingness handling, and routing rules; they do not establish clinical validity, deployment safety, or natural-failure prevalence.

title: Stretched bilayer-cytoskeleton links hold echinocytes in a model splenic slit
comment: 35 pages, 8 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Materials included (pages S1-S16, 6 figures, 1 table); Movies S1 to S3 are ancillary files. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Stored red blood cells become echinocytes, growing spicules before losing membrane; the spleen clears the resulting small, spherical cells. Whether spicules alone hinder splenic passage is unknown. Shape and area change together. In a two-component model whose shrinking cytoskeleton raises spicules, we drove a discocyte and stage I to III echinocytes of equal area and volume through a model splenic slit. The pressure drop needed to pass rose with stage; stage III echinocytes were held at 37 to 50 times the pressure drop that passed the discocyte. Bilayer-cytoskeleton links stretched near full extension held these cells; lengthening them about twofold released a held cell. Capillary-sized channels, as in our device, separated the stages far less. Of the shape classes in stored blood, the model held at high pressure drops only storage-induced microerythrocytes, which perfused human spleens clear most. Spicules, besides membrane loss, may decide which stored cells the spleen retains.

title: Turbulent velocity statistics in convective boundary layers
summary: Large-eddy simulations (LES) of the convective atmospheric boundary layer (CBL) are used to investigate velocity variance statistics in turbulent sheared convection. The thirteen simulations span conditions from weak convection with longitudinal rolls to free penetrative convection with no mean wind. In the presence of thermal rolls, the near-surface streamwise variance profile exhibits an approximately logarithmic decay with a slope proportional to the friction velocity, $u_*$, and an added constant proportional to the convective velocity, $w_\star$. After the structural transition to convective cells, both the streamwise and spanwise variances follow the empirical stability and height dependencies of Wilson (\textit{Boundary-Layer Meteorol.}, 2008, vol. 129, pp. 353--369). The near-surface vertical (wall-normal) velocity variance is well described by Monin--Obukhov similarity with improved agreement using local-in-height scaling. Within the mixed layer, the peak vertical variance initially decreases relative to $w_\star$ as shear diminishes, before increasing and shifting downward as the flow approaches free convection. In contrast, the total turbulent energy decreases relative to $w_\star$ across the parameter space. The spanwise velocity variance represents the dominant turbulent component under weak convection and exceeds the streamwise variance throughout most of the convective regime. These statistical trends are attributed to the role of pressure, evaluated through variance budget contributions. Large-scale buoyancy production in the mixed layer is transported downward by pressure and redistributed preferentially to the spanwise component, coinciding with the presence of longitudinal roll motions. The weakening of this pressure-transport pathway for convective cells coincides with greater retention of vertical variance within the mixed layer.

title: Supervision-Aware Evaluation of MedGemma for Reference-Assisted Radiotherapy Contour Ranking
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
summary: Radiotherapy contour ranking can support quality assurance, but vision-language model (VLM) gains may reflect supervision, score construction, available inputs, or representation access. We evaluated frozen MedGemma 1.5 in a single-institution study, a 12-patient held-out HaN-Seg test, five-fold cross-fitting on 30 non-test HaN-Seg patients, and transfer without refitting to 120 SegRap2023 patients. On held-out HaN-Seg, a supervised readout of the final prompt state exceeded a supervised readout of the model's yes/no output probabilities by +0.3047 pooled average precision (AP; 95% patient-bootstrap interval [+0.2822, +0.3269]); the advantage persisted against a parameter-count-matched nonlinear control. A readout of projected visual tokens exceeded the final-state readout in cross-fitting and transfer (+0.0706 AP averaged equally across patients on SegRap; 95% interval [+0.0607, +0.0804]), while a structured panel-feature readout remained competitive with visual tokens. The anatomy-conditioned readout did not demonstrate an advantage over the native-feature comparator. These results motivate visual-token and structured-feature controls in medical-imaging VLM evaluations; outcomes were computational or synthetic, not clinical acceptability.

title: Thermal convection and jets produced by human exhalation dominate the indoor spreading of emitted CO$_2$ and aerosols
comment: 22 pages (main text 9 pages + Supplementary Information 13 pages), 14 figures, 4 tables
summary: For understanding airborne viral infection pathways, the prediction of the spreading and effective diffusivity of saliva droplets emitted from a person while speaking and breathing is crucial. In non-ventilated indoor spaces, the spreading of tracer particles or molecules emitted by a person is governed by the complex interplay of molecular diffusion, convection due to body heat and temperature boundary conditions as well as propulsion due to breathing in and out. By comparison of grid-based simulations of the compressible Navier-Stokes equation with experiments measuring the spreading of CO$_2$ emitted from a person, we demonstrate that molecular diffusion of CO$_2$ is present, but that the long-distance CO$_2$ spreading is completely dominated by the combination of convection due to body heat and temperature gradients at walls and windows and the periodic breathing pattern of a person. Breathing out induces long-range advection by a mid-Reynolds number flow pattern akin to the Landau-Squire jet, while breathing in creates only short-range flow. In conjunction with thermal convection, this symmetry breaking between breathing in and out produces fast long-distance transport of CO$_2$ and small aerosols.

title: Melting Ice Activates Mechanical Forcing from Entrapped Air
summary: Natural ice commonly contains entrapped air, yet its dynamical role during melting remains unresolved. Using numerical simulations and theoretical analysis, we show that melt-front-released bubbles activate entrapped air as a mechanical forcing on the liquid. Bubble buoyancy disrupts density-anomaly-induced thermal structure and injects momentum into the melt-controlling boundary layer, producing melt rates more than twice the bubble-free value at percent-level gas fractions. The evolving interface and background convection regulate this coupling, which weakens again under sufficiently vigorous convection, producing a finite coupling window. A mechanical-power ratio comparing bubble-generated and background-flow power organizes this behavior. Recasting the bubble contribution as an effective near-boundary velocity extends standard ice-ocean melt closures, while reported field conditions can enter the mechanically significant regime. More broadly, a moving phase boundary can activate an embedded dispersed phase as an internal mechanical forcing.

title: HR-NVC++: Unified Ultra-High-Resolution Neural Video Coding with Confidence-Guided Spatial-Temporal Cues
summary: Ultra-high-resolution neural video coding (NVC) remains challenging because temporal correspondence becomes increasingly unreliable as spatial resolution increases. Although recent neural B-frame codecs have improved bi-directional temporal prediction, complex motion and fine-grained structures still lead to unreliable temporal references, while spatial information of the current frame remains underexploited. In this work, we propose HR-NVC++, a unified ultra-high-resolution NVC approach that supports both fidelity-oriented and perceptual-quality-oriented compression with a shared spatial-temporal context. The context integrates bi-directional temporal cues with complementary spatial information: confidence-guided fusion adaptively balances the forward and backward temporal cues according to their estimated correspondence reliability, while a spatial complement branch enriches regions that temporal references fail to explain. The resulting context serves as a common basis for two compression modes. Built upon this shared context, the fidelity mode retains entropy-based latent coding for pixel-accurate compression, whereas the perceptual mode removes additional latent coding and performs reconstruction directly from the context. This design demonstrates that a sufficiently informative spatial-temporal context already carries the dominant content required for perceptually favorable reconstruction, allowing different compression objectives to share the same contextual representation. Extensive experiments on UVG-4K and JVET Class A1/A2 show that HR-NVC++ achieves an average PSNR BD-rate saving of 13.01% over the H.266/VVC reference model VTM-13.2 under the random access configuration, while delivering substantially better perceptual quality and temporal consistency than existing neural video codecs.

title: Silscore: modelling siRNA potency with positional thermodynamics and data-selected nucleotide-identity terms
comment: 25 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) enable programmable gene silencing, but candidates targeting the same transcript can differ markedly in potency. Existing predictors range from interpretable empirical rules with limited accuracy to high-capacity models that can lose performance when datasets or targets change. We present Silscore, a guide-only model that combines a quadratic preference for overall duplex stability, a position-resolved profile of nearest-neighbour stacking energies and sparse nucleotide-identity terms selected from residuals left unexplained by thermodynamics. Its main fit uses 26 parameters, fewer than half as many as any trainable comparator evaluated here. We evaluate Silscore on the canonical split of the Huesken dataset, two external datasets (Mixset and Katoh-Suzuki), and an evaluation in which the same guides are tested after training on dissimilar targets. Silscore attains the highest observed Pearson correlation in all three transfer evaluations, and the data support an advantage over every applicable comparator on Katoh-Suzuki. For a fixed evaluation set, we compare two equally sized training sets with higher or lower sequence similarity to the evaluation sequences. After training on the less similar sequences, Silscore has the highest observed correlation, and the data do not establish a change in its performance. The fitted parameters can also be interpreted directly: identity terms locate sequence effects that base-pairing energies cannot express, global stability has a data-estimated intermediate optimum, and local energy profiles recover terminal asymmetry and a preference for weaker seed and stronger central pairing. Silscore thus provides a compact, data-driven model that combines strong predictive performance with robustness when tested in new settings and expresses previously reported empirical preferences as quantities estimated from data.

title: Moment-matching closure models for Taylor dispersion
summary: Shear dispersion is important in contaminant transport, chemical separation and microfluidic applications. The classical Taylor model describes the long-time spreading of the cross-sectional mean field but does not generally capture its earlier evolution. This work presents a moment-matched closure for steady parallel flows with arbitrary smooth velocity profiles and transversely uniform initial scalar fields. Expanding the exact response of the scalar fluctuations, we construct a Krylov basis combining the leading high-frequency direction with selected temporal and spatial low-frequency directions. Using this basis, we apply orthogonal projection and a quasi-steady (QS) approximation of the unresolved response to obtain a coupled system of advection-diffusion equations for the mean field and reduced variables. We establish well-posedness and energy stability, give sufficient conditions for mean-field convergence, and show that the QS correction improves the low-frequency approximation. Tests in two-dimensional periodic shear flow and Poiseuille pipe flow show accurate mean-field predictions from the initial transients towards the Taylor limit, with rapid error reduction as more reduced variables are retained.

title: Physics-based simulation unlocks scaling laws for generalizable MRI reconstruction
summary: Deep-learning-based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction holds great promise for accelerating acquisitions, yet its clinical translation remains bottlenecked by poor generalizability across unseen scanners, populations, anatomies, and protocols. Gathering sufficiently diverse clinical datasets to overcome this bottleneck is hindered by high acquisition costs, privacy restrictions, and institutional biases. Here, we introduce Scalable Inverse Model (SIM), a framework that systematically co-designs physics-simulated training data, model architecture, and learning paradigms around scalability--leveraging compute scaling to overcome historical data bottlenecks and achieve robust zero-shot MRI reconstruction. Across 14 public and in-house datasets--spanning seven international centers, five vendors, field strengths of 0.3-7 T, over ten anatomical regions, more than ten acquisition protocols, downstream quantitative and molecular tasks, and a 150-scan blinded radiologist study--SIM demonstrates robust zero-shot generalizability, recovering fine anatomical details while suppressing aliasing artifacts where conventional deep-learning methods fail. Attention-map analyses confirm that SIM learns physically explainable, dynamically adaptive reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors. SIM establishes a scalable, privacy-preserving, and democratized infrastructure for universal MRI reconstruction, providing a blueprint for generalizable AI across inverse problems in medical imaging.

title: Transient CFD simulation of a linear start-up of a variable speed reversible pump-turbine
comment: Conference paper presented at IAHR-SHMS 2026, 33rd Symposium on Hydraulic Machinery and Systems
summary: The integration of intermittent energy sources has led to a growing demand for fast response and partial-load operation of hydraulic turbines, making variable speed units increasingly important. In hydraulic turbines, frequent start-stop cycles generate the highest loads under normal operating conditions. Although historically infrequent and often neglected in turbine design, the growing occurrence of these cycles now necessitates particular consideration due to their contribution to fatigue loading and reduced runner lifetime. Experimental investigations of turbine start-up are costly and cannot be conducted during early design stages. While start-up sequences have been simulated with CFD for fixed speed turbines, each approach has had notable limitations. Some studies have lacked experimental validation. Some studies have used reduced geometrical domains, making it unclear whether inaccuracies stem from geometry simplification or turbulence modelling, and others employ hybrid LES/RANS models, at a very high computational cost, making them unfeasible for use during the design phase. In this study, the linear start-up of a variable-speed turbine start-up is simulated using URANS-based approaches. Simulations are performed using the k-$ω$ SST, EARSM, and the RSM turbulence models within a computationally tractable framework. The simulations show that torque, mass flow, and the blade-passing frequency content at the leading edge are accurately captured by all models. In contrast, the frequency content at the trailing edge and in the draft tube is considerably better resolved using the RSM than the other models because of its capability to consistently capture turbulence anisotropy.

title: FGCARL: Fisher-Guided Continuously Adaptive Representation Learning for Medical Image Segmentation
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures
summary: Deep learning (DL) has achieved remarkable success in medical image segmentation by learning data-driven representations from large-scale annotated datasets. However, medical images are often collected independently across clinical sites, resulting in substantial domain shifts due to differences in imaging modalities, acquisition protocols, and intensity distributions. Meanwhile, segmentation classes may vary across sites due to differences in annotation standards, leading to class shifts. These evolving domains and class definitions can substantially degrade segmentation performance on newly encountered data, while sequential adaptation may cause catastrophic forgetting of knowledge acquired from previously encountered domains and classes. Existing incremental learning methods for medical image segmentation primarily address either domain shifts or class shifts, with these two settings largely investigated independently. This separation leaves a critical gap in developing a unified approach that can simultaneously adapt to evolving domains and newly introduced classes while retaining previously acquired knowledge. To address this challenge, we propose Fisher-Guided Continuously Adaptive Representation Learning, a unified framework for domain- and class-incremental 3D volumetric medical image segmentation. FGCARL comprises two key components: Mutual Adaptive Instance Representation (MAIR), which adaptively aligns feature distributions across sequentially encountered domains through bidirectional normalization and denormalization, and Fisher-Guided Knowledge Retention (FGKR), which selectively preserves parameters important for previously learned domains and classes through Fisher-guided regularization. Experimental results demonstrate that FGCARL consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods, effectively adapting to domain and class shifts while mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

title: Boundary-layer detachment and infinite-Reynolds limit of two-dimensional wall-bounded flows
comment: 34 pages, 11 figures
summary: Understanding boundary-layer detachment and its consequences for the infinite-Reynolds-number limit remains a major challenge in fluid mechanics. Here, direct numerical simulations of incompressible flow in a two-dimensional periodic channel with no-slip walls are used to investigate this problem. Reynolds-number-dependent initial conditions are constructed with a boundary layer of Prandtl thickness that converge in the energy norm to an analytic, stationary Euler flow, while the associated Prandtl system develops a finite-time singularity. Highly resolved simulations show boundary-layer detachment and departures from Prandtl scaling, yet provide numerical evidence that the Navier--Stokes solutions continue to converge to the Euler flow over the simulated time interval. In particular, the squared energy norm of the velocity difference and the time-averaged energy dissipation both scale approximately as $Re^{-1/2}$, consistently with established convergence criteria. Although the detached vortices become more numerous and intense as the Reynolds number increases, their characteristic size and occupied area appear to decrease. These observations suggest how boundary-layer detachment and the breakdown of the Prandtl description can coexist with convergence to a smooth Euler flow.

title: CODE-PIF: Convex/Deep (CODE) Multiview Pseudoinvariant Features for Multitemporal Multispectral Surface Reflectance Imagery
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures
summary: Multitemporal multispectral surface reflectance imagery exhibits radiometric and spectral variability due to atmospheric effects, sensor differences, and actual surface changes, complicating the identification of pseudoinvariant features (PIFs). The SOTA DeepMGCCA captures nonlinear dependencies across acquisition dates, but similarity in its learned feature space does not directly establish consistency in the original reflectance domain. Meanwhile, we believe that the PIFs extracted by DeepMGCCA preserve essential structural characteristics, providing an effective prior to guide subsequent refinement. Therefore, we propose the CODE-PIF architecture, an unsupervised convex/deep (CODE) framework that refines the coarse PIF from DeepMGCCA using convex optimization. Specifically, CODE-PIF uses the data-fitting term to integrate reflectance deviations, correlation-weighted spectral angles, and temporal reference change information to promote radiometric and spectral consistency between predicted PIFs and observed data. Moreover, the regularization term uses a mathematically simple Q-quadratic norm to incorporate information from the coarse PIF estimate into the refined solution. The resulting convex optimization problem is solved using the ADMM optimizer, which decomposes it into simpler subproblems and provides convergence guarantees under standard assumptions. Experiments across four distinct ROIs show improved average radiometric and spectral agreement relative to DeepMGCCA.Averaged across these regions, the RMSE decreases from 0.0192 to 0.0164, PSNR increases from 35.91 to 37.44 dB, and the between-date spectral angle decreases from 3.77 to 2.97 degrees. Although structural similarity and Pearson correlation do not improve in every scene, the results suggest that using observed data helps select PIFs with more consistent reflectance values and spectral shapes across dates.

title: Extension of the Renard-Deck Drag Decomposition to Compressible Rough-Wall Turbulent Boundary Layers
comment: 33 pages, 15 figures, 6 tables
summary: A generalized Renard-Deck (RD) drag decomposition is developed for spatially developing compressible turbulent boundary layers over rough surfaces. Derived from the locally resolved, time-averaged momentum equations, the formulation accounts for both viscous friction and pressure drag without requiring spatial averaging at the roughness-element scale. Eight direct numerical simulations are considered at freestream Mach numbers of 2.5 and 5.86, comparing smooth walls and two-dimensional transverse square ribs ($λ_x/k=8$) under adiabatic and cold-wall conditions. The decomposition reconstructs the total drag with errors below 5%. Mean-flow viscous dissipation and turbulent kinetic-energy production together account for approximately 90% of the drag work. While their contributions are comparable over smooth walls, turbulent production dominates over rough walls, contributing approximately 80%. More importantly, roughness substantially alters the wall-normal distributions of both contributions. Viscous dissipation becomes concentrated near the roughness crest, whereas turbulent production peaks above the crest, with both contributions decaying more gradually into the outer layer than over smooth walls. The resulting differences in their cumulative contributions persist across a substantial fraction of the boundary layer, demonstrating that the energetic influence of surface roughness extends well beyond the roughness sublayer.

title: Transmission-Mode Multispectral Imaging for Estimation of Microcystis spp. Cell Concentration and ELISA-Equivalent Microcystin Concentration in Water
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Includes Supplementary Information
summary: Harmful algal blooms dominated by Microcystis spp. threaten freshwater systems through proliferation and microcystin (MC) production. Conventional measurements of cyanobacterial abundance and MC concentration commonly require laboratory processing, specialized instrumentation, or assay reagents. Because MC concentration cannot always be reliably inferred from cell abundance, complementary optical approaches for estimating both quantities are of interest. This study proposes and evaluates a transmission mode multispectral imaging (MSI) framework for estimating Microcystis spp. cell concentration and ELISA-equivalent MC concentration from culture derived dilution samples. A custom built MSI system acquiring twelve spectral bands from near-ultraviolet to near-infrared wavelengths measured transmitted light spectral responses. Following principal component analysis based dimensionality reduction, spectral variation was quantified using an aggregated Wasserstein distance descriptor for regression based prediction. Cell concentration estimation yielded $R^2=0.9819$ for calibration and $R^2=0.9754$ on held-out intermediate dilution levels, while ELISA-equivalent MC estimation yielded $R^2=0.9788$ for calibration and $R^2=0.9786$ on held-out intermediate dilution levels. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transmission-mode MSI as a dual output optical calibration framework for estimation of Microcystis spp. cell concentration and ELISA-equivalent MC concentration in water.

title: Hypersonic Flow Over an Axisymmetric Open Cavity: Effects of Segmentation Angle and Reynolds Number
comment: 14 Figures. The article is yet to be submitted to a journal
summary: This study investigates the influence of cavity segmentation angle ($φ$) on the flow characteristics of a cavity mounted on a cone under Mach 6 freestream conditions in a Ludwieg tunnel. Four segmentation configurations, corresponding to $φ= 360^\circ$, $48^\circ$, $32^\circ$, and $16^\circ$, are examined for cavity length-to-depth ratios ($L/D$) of 1 and 6 over a range of Reynolds numbers ($Re_D = 23000$--$74000$). The flow field is characterized using surface pressure and heat flux measurements, complemented by planar laser Rayleigh scattering visualization. The results indicate that, for $L/D = 1$, the downstream Strouhal number ($St$) and mean pressure remain largely unaffected by the segmentation angle and closely agree with those of the axisymmetric configuration. In contrast, the flow parameters within the cavity are larger than in the axisymmetric case, which is attributed to the three-dimensional bounding effect. For $L/D = 6$, the mean pressure distribution exhibits a similar trend across the segmentation angles, whereas the downstream $St$ increases with increasing $φ$, approaching the axisymmetric value. Flow-mode transitions are observed across all segmentation angles, consistent with the axisymmetric configuration. However, both the transition Reynolds numbers and the corresponding flow modes vary with the segmentation angle.

title: Data Archive for 2D and 3D Electrical Impedance Tomography with moderate conductivity contrast phantoms
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures. Data available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24120439
summary: This document describes open Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) measurement data that were collected from biomedical imaging inspired phantoms with moderate conductivity contrasts. The data were collected with the KIT4 and KIT5 EIT measurement devices at the University of Eastern Finland, and are intended for EIT image reconstruction algorithm development and testing. The data from thoracic imaging inspired cylindrical and chest-shaped phantoms are suitable for 2D algorithms, and the data from an intracerebral hemorrhage imaging inspired head-shaped phantom with resistive skull are suitable for 3D algorithms. In addition to the measurement data, computational meshes and example reconstruction codes are provided and sample reconstructions included.

title: Divergent Interfacial Lifetimes without Bulk Criticality in Fully Miscible Fluids
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures; Supplemental Material available as an ancillary file
summary: A fully miscible interface must disappear at equilibrium, but its lifetime need not be governed by a bulk instability. We construct a spatially resolved, dissipative two-field model in which a prepared correlation-excited interface undergoes a localized saddle-node while its homogeneous excited surroundings remain metastable and the relaxed mixture is strictly one phase. The interfacial soft mode produces a deterministic first-passage time that grows as the inverse square root of the distance from the fold and couples directly to the evolving concentration-profile width. The quartic structural potential admits an exact reduction from competing positive harmonic energies on a constrained configuration manifold; sixth- and eighth-order examples provide additional numerical robustness tests. The result is an interface-specific kinetic singularity without equilibrium bulk criticality, subject to explicitly stated microscopic and continuum limits.
