title: Flow Structure in Idealized Rotating Detonation Combustor with Supersonic Inflow
summary: The work presented investigates the flow structure and stability of an airbreathing rotating detonation engine (RDE) in an idealized combustor. The presented derivation of a modified pressure cutoff injection scheme allows for supersonic injection in an idealized two-dimensional RDE as a function of a specified design Mach number and the pressure ratio across the injection surface. Numerical simulations are conducted using a compressible reacting flow solver with finite-rate chemistry built on an Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) framework. The fuel mixture is set to a stoichiometric hydrogen-air mixture for all simulations. Stable operation occurs for a wide range of inflow conditions with inflow Mach numbers up to 4. The increased total temperature associated with increasing Mach numbers causes burning at the injection surface during the injector recovery process, resulting in unstable operation. Meanwhile, increasing total pressure facilitates sustained supersonic injection. Analysis of the steady flow structure shows a familiar structure with significant changes to the detonation structure when compared with a rocket RDE. With supersonic inflow, an oblique detonation wave (ODW) forms along the injection surface connected to the moving detonation through a slip line. Changes in the oblique detonation wave and normal detonation angle occur with changes in the inflow Mach number, however the overall detonation structure remains similar when supersonic injection occurs.

title: Data-driven Correction Reduced-Order Stochastic Collocation Method for the Time-Dependent Navier-Stokes Equations
comment: 23 pages, 10 figures
summary:
We develop two hybrid data-driven Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) Reduced-Order Models (ROMs) for the non-stationary incompressible Navier--Stokes Equations (NSEs) with random viscosity. The proposed framework combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) ROMs, spatial filtering, data-driven closure modeling, and the Stochastic Collocation Method (SCM). A key feature is the approximation of the realization-dependent closure term by the closure associated with the expected viscosity. Consequently, a single data-driven closure model constructed from the full-order solution corresponding to the expected viscosity can be reused across all realizations, thereby avoiding the expensive construction of realization-specific closure models. This leads to the Data-Driven Correction UQ ROM (DDC-UQ-ROM) and its physically constrained variant, the Constrained DDC-UQ-ROM (CDDC-UQ-ROM), in which physical constraints are imposed on the data-driven correction model.
  The proposed methods are evaluated for a two-dimensional (2D) flow past a circular cylinder problem with a 5D random viscosity field, considering mean Reynolds numbers $Re=100$ and $Re=500$, different correlation lengths, and both in-sample and out-of-sample parameter settings. Numerical results show that the DDC-UQ-ROM generally improves upon the standard Galerkin ROM (G-ROM), while the CDDC-UQ-ROM exhibits the most accurate and robust approximation of the benchmark energy evolution across the cases considered. The robustness and accuracy of the CDDC-UQ-ROM are further assessed through statistical error analyses of the first- and second-order energy moments, reduced-training-data experiments, and an indicative comparison of wall-clock computational costs with the full-order UQ calculations.

title: Three-body streaming forces lower the axial binding threshold of a held transverse three-sphere chain
comment: 19 pages including supplementary material, 5 figures
summary: Particles in oscillatory liquids can form chains perpendicular to the drive. We ask whether the forces between isolated pairs predict when three spheres can bind at a finite spacing. We first hold the spheres fixed during small-amplitude oscillation and calculate the cycle-averaged force on an end sphere. The three-body contribution lowers the critical Stokes number from 4.283 for the pair-additive model to 3.534 for the full chain, a reduction of 17.5 percent. An independent finite-element calculation reproduces the shift. The three-body attraction also draws the spheres close enough for the nearest-neighbour pair forces to become repulsive. This compression accounts for most of the tendency to bend out of the plane containing the drive and the chain. For freely translating and rotating spheres at a particle-to-liquid density ratio of 2.2, the multipole calculation predicts initial growth of this bend at five sampled equilibria. A point-singularity calculation confirms the sign at two of those spacings.

title: Gradient-Aware AI Agents for Autonomous Turbulence Model Discovery via Differentiable CFD
summary: Turbulence modeling relies on human choices of closure form, physical inputs, and tunable parameters. Training closures a posteriori is efficient only with gradients through long chaotic rollouts, which few solvers provide. Most a posteriori approaches therefore resort to gradient-free optimization, and nearly all fix the closure form in advance, learning only its parameters. In this work, we introduce a gradient-aware agentic framework that poses closure discovery as a bilevel problem: a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system searches over closure forms, while a GPU-native differentiable computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver supplies gradients, making differentiable a posteriori learning an action of the autonomous AI agent. For each proposal, the agents construct a differentiable training program by embedding the analytical, neural, or hybrid closure in the solver, implementing a differentiable objective, and validating the gradient path. They then decide whether to evaluate the closure, compute its parameter sensitivities, or train it a posteriori, select the optimization settings, and revise subsequent proposals using the simulation outcomes and returned gradients. Truncated-horizon gradients make this training usable under chaotic dynamics for closures with tens of thousands of parameters. Demonstrations include dissipation-law and subgrid-scale closure discovery in two-dimensional turbulence and wall-model discovery for large-eddy simulation of three-dimensional channel flow. With gradient-based training, the agent recovers reference coefficients that forward evaluation alone does not reach within the same budget, and autonomously discovers and trains analytical and neural closures that improve agreement with the targeted reference statistics. These results demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end autonomous turbulence model development in time-resolved flows.

title: A thermodynamically consistent, fully compressible, fluctuating hydrodynamics model of a Cahn Hilliard binary fluid mixture
comment: 80 pages, 1 figure
summary: We derive, from first principles, a thermodynamically consistent set of fully compressible fluctuating hydrodynamic equations for a Cahn-Hilliard binary fluid mixture, in isothermal and non-isothermal form and for symmetric and non-symmetric mixtures. The derivation uses the GENERIC formalism, with the friction operator constructed from flux fluctuations following Jelic and Ottinger, so that deterministic and stochastic fluxes derive from the same operator and correlation matrix and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem holds by construction. We show that the momentum equation must use the total mass density, that the Cahn-Hilliard variable is the mass fraction, and that the diffusion flux must be driven by the specific, not the volumetric, exchange potential. We derive a generalized Korteweg tensor for square-gradient energies in density and composition, and show that the reversible pressure tensor of the non-isothermal model is fixed by the degeneracy condition, producing a thermal capillary stress when the interfacial free energy has an entropic part. Thermodynamic consistency is proved in full: Jacobi identity, positivity and degeneracy, local energy conservation with interstitial-working fluxes, a local entropy balance, Soret-Dufour reciprocity, and Einstein statistics of the linearized equations. The final equations are written in conservative form for finite-volume discretization, and closed-form static and dynamic structure factors are given for all models as analytic benchmarks. An appendix shows that the same models follow from classical irreversible thermodynamics with the Helmholtz or Gibbs free energy; this route is unique for isothermal flows and has a gauge freedom in the non-isothermal case that GENERIC removes.

title: Generative AI models for exploring diffusion dynamics from multi-frame particle tracking
summary: Particle-based volumetric flow measurement techniques have proven their efficacy in quantitatively assessing the dynamic characteristics of unsteady flows within the realm of fluid mechanics. Despite recent advances in multi-frame particle tracking, an open challenge in this area is maintaining trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences, where inter-frame displacements are large. In this work, we develop DiffTR-Flow3D, a diffusion-based model that estimates flow motion from spatiotemporal three-dimensional particle recordings via a stochastic diffusion process. DiffTR-Flow3D conditions the diffusion process with both global and local particle dynamics and enhances flow estimation by leveraging historical particle trajectories. Extensive experiments, including numerical simulations and real-world measurements, demonstrate that DiffTR-Flow3D achieves state-of-the-art displacement estimation accuracy compared with learning-based flow estimators, and, when integrated into particle tracking pipelines, substantially improves their long-term tracking performance, while exhibiting robustness and generalization across diverse flow patterns. This work is expected to provide fluid researchers with an effective tool for the consistent and precise analysis of particle trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences with large inter-frame displacements.

title: A linear stability method based on generalized hydrodynamics: application to high-speed plane Couette flow beyond continuum regime
comment: 42 pages, 16 figures
summary: Linear stability analysis of compressible shear flows beyond continuum regime attracts increasing attention in recent years accounting for high-altitude applications. In this paper, the temporal stability of high-speed plane Couette flow in near-continuum regime is addressed. A novel linear stability method based on the generalized hydrodynamic equations (GHE) with slip boundary conditions is developed within the 13-moment framework. Meanwhile, the linear stability equations of the nonlinear coupled constitutive relations (NCCR) and the Navier--Stokes (NS) equations are also given. Based on the developed methods, the linear stability of plane Couette flows at $Ma=2.5$--10 and $Kn=2.7\times 10^{-5}$--0.07 are analyzed, and the rarefaction effects on the base flow, eigenspectrum, mode synchronization and least stable mode are investigated. The results show that the GHE with slip boundary conditions agrees well with direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) results in predicting base flow profiles of velocity, temperature, all stress and heat flux components, while the NS equations show considerable differences, especially for capturing the nonlinear normal stress and tangential heat flux. The GHE-based linear stability theory (LST) recovers to the classical NS-based LST in the continuum limit, while they show considerable differences when $Kn$ reaches $O(0.01)$. As rarefaction degree increases, the synchronization between acoustic modes and viscous modes becomes weak, and all modes become stable in rarefied plane Couette flow. The surface slip effect and nonlinear transport increase the disturbance phase speeds, while they have different effects on the growth rate of different modes. Generally, rarefaction effects increase the growth rate of the least stable Mode II at low wavenumbers, and show more pronounced effects on higher modes and high-wavenumber disturbances.

title: Lifetime of localized turbulence in transitional channel flow
summary: The lifetime of localized turbulence in transitional channel flow, the so-called turbulent stripes or bands, as a function of the Reynolds number ($Re$) is reported here. Recent studies showed that although the mean lifetime of a turbulent band increases with the band length, it appears to saturate at a certain critical length, which is smaller than the fully developed band length. However, this observation was based on a single Reynolds number only. Here, we first confirmed this saturation by considering higher Reynolds numbers. This property enables us to measure the characteristic lifetime of a turbulent band without having to resolve it at its full length, which greatly reduces the computational cost and makes statistical studies by direct numerical simulation (DNS) feasible near the lower end of the transitional-$Re$ regime. Subsequently, by extensive DNS, we measured the lifetime up to $Re=670$, and the data cover more than two orders of magnitude, ranging from $O(10^2)$ to nearly $O(10^5)$ and revealing a sharp but smooth growth with increasing $Re$. No sudden divergence of the lifetime was observed in the $Re$ range investigated, in which controversy existed over whether or not a turbulent band would become sustained. Despite significant differences between the structure and dynamics of channel bands and pipe puffs, our data concretely support a unified transition scenario in the two flows.

title: Shallow water equations on n-dimensional Riemannian manifolds: a kinetic approach
comment: 38 pages. 5 figures
summary: We develop an intrinsic kinetic moment closure for shallow-water equations on smooth manifolds of arbitrary dimension equipped with prescribed, possibly time-dependent Riemannian metrics. Hamiltonian transport on the cotangent bundle and metric-dependent momentum integration yield balance laws with hydrostatic pressure, bottom topography, a skew-adjoint force, and dissipative bottom friction. An explicit compactly supported Gibbs equilibrium satisfies the required mass, momentum, and tensor second-moment conditions. We derive the quasilinear formulation and characteristic speeds, establish the continuous mechanical-energy balance with geometric work and frictional dissipation, and obtain a weak entropy inequality for vanishing-viscosity limits under stated convergence assumptions. On the rotating sphere with a fixed round metric, the skew-adjoint force represents Coriolis effects. We construct a kinetic finite-volume scheme combining local fluxes, hydrostatic reconstruction, and geometric source terms. A second-order time integrator uses independently restricted steps at its two Euler stages. The scheme conserves discrete water volume, preserves nonnegative depth under a sufficient CFL condition, and is well balanced for lakes at rest, including wet/dry interfaces. Six-hour simulations of a localized surface disturbance over Earth topography with Manning bottom friction maintain positive depths and conserve water volume to near machine precision. Comparison with a spherical central-upwind method shows similar surface-wave propagation and gauge time series, with remaining differences in late-time local extrema.

title: SUMNO: Spatially Unrolled Multigrid Neural Operator for Fluid Flow Surrogates
comment: 37 pages, 6 figures
summary: Data-driven surrogate modeling has emerged as a powerful paradigm for accelerating computational fluid dynamics, and hierarchical U-shaped networks, which resemble the structure of classical Geometric Multigrid (GMG) methods, have become prevalent designs. Modern surrogates built on these designs achieve competitive accuracy at a fraction of the cost of numerical solvers; however, accurate prediction of complex flows remains challenging, and no existing architecture leads across them. In such networks, the multigrid analogy mainly concerns the multi-resolution topology, while their components largely follow common vision practice. To address this, this study introduces SUMNO, a multigrid neural operator for fluid flow fields on regular grids that spatially unrolls a V-cycle into a feed-forward U-shaped network. Parameter-free down- and upsampling stand in for restriction and prolongation, and additive skip connections for coarse-grid correction, with normalization-free transfer and skip pathways. Within this macro-architecture, convolutions are used at the fine and intermediate resolutions and shifted-window attention at the coarsest, whose window partitioning is generalized to handle periodicity independently per axis. Evaluated on unseen test configurations across four unsteady and steady flow benchmarks against five representative baselines, SUMNO is best in 5 of 7 settings and ranks second in the remaining two. It reduces the 10-step rollout MSE by about 30% relative to the strongest baseline, and outperforms three baselines with over 130 million parameters using 9.4 million parameters.

title: Variational Newton-Krylov descent for periodic orbits of two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow
comment: 42 pages, 18 figures, 5 tables. Supplementary material (catalogue of the solutions) as an ancillary file. Submitted to the Journal of Fluid Mechanics
summary: A matrix-free Newton-Krylov method for computing long unstable periodic orbits of turbulent flows is presented. The method arises from the space-time variational formulation of Lan & Cvitanović (Phys. Rev. E, vol. 69, 2004, 016217), and runs on graphics processing units with a preconditioner from time-spectral methods that retains advection. In two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow at $Re = 40$, near recurrences remain about as frequent at long periods as at moderate ones, and searches from them converge to 183 distinct solutions with periods up to 191, about forty escape times, all but one verified by multiple shooting. The primary question is then whether such a long orbit can be taken, on its own, as a proxy for the attractor, and thus capture the statistics of the turbulent flow. The mean dissipation and energy of the long orbits lie close to the medians of the flow, and the distribution of the dissipation along a long orbit is comparable with that of a turbulent segment of the same duration, except in its tail, which most orbits miss. Their leading Floquet exponents appear to lie slightly below the Lyapunov spectrum of the flow, as may be expected of quieter orbits. The typical distance of the turbulent flow from a long orbit decreases as the period grows, but with an unfavourable scaling set by the correlation dimension of the attractor, which suggests that ever longer orbits may be needed as the Reynolds number grows.

title: Experimental and numerical simulations of near resonant 2D soliton interaction in shallow water
comment: accepted for publication for Water Waves
summary: Experiments were carried out in {a} large wave basin ($27\times 30$\,m$^2$) to study the interactions of non-linear waves in shallow water (0.35\,m deep). A stereoscopic technique was used to measure the waves accurately over a vast area ($180$\,m$^2$). The numerical code {Tolosa-lct}, designed for simulating wave propagation in shallow water, reproduces the observations and extends the analysis for larger domains. The diffraction of oblique solitons is discussed. Mach interaction of two solitons occurs for some given incidence and amplitudes, producing a third soliton. A focus is made on the near resonant interaction of a soliton with a vertical wall. An example of a regular Mach interaction is shown, where a steady solution is achieved experimentally, with a maximum amplitude amplification of 3.2 at the wall.

title: Access to the quasi-geostrophic model from within the BK19 compressible flow solver
comment: To appear in https://msp.org/soon/coming.php?jpath=camcos
summary: We extend BK19 the semi-implicit finite-volume solver, to provide access to the quasi-geostrophic (QG) regime within the same compressible framework that already admits soundproof and hydrostatic limits. In order to achieve this goal, we incorporate the asymptotic framework from the continuous theory into the numerical scheme. Adopting the usual asymptotic setting for the quasi-geostrophic regime and using it directly in the numerical model, we perform a scale analysis of the compressible Euler equations in the synoptic length and time scales in the limit of small Rossby number. In this limit, the discrete implicit step recovers geostrophic balance, together with the pseudo-incompressible divergence constraint. We construct a staggered-grid curl operator consistent with the discrete derivatives and use it to define the vorticity in the numerical framework. An asymptotic analysis of the fully discrete scheme then yields a Poisson-type equation for the leading-order Exner-pressure perturbation that coincides with the QG pressure Poisson equation in the continuous theory. As a result of this analysis, we introduce two additional blending switches that (i) convert the elliptic pressure problem from the full Helmholtz to its QG Poisson-type equation and (ii) control whether the horizontal momenta are updated prognostically or diagnosed from geostrophic balance. In combination with the existing soundproof and hydrostatic switches, the resulting algorithm can be operated in fully compressible, pseudo-incompressible, hydrostatic, and QG modes without changing the underlying discretization. The functionality of the numerical scheme in the QG regime is then tested by two idealized vortex test cases to show how stable the vortices remain in the QG run and that, as the Rossby number is reduced, the full compressible scheme converges to slow, balanced QG dynamics.

title: Rotationally Symmetric Lattice Boltzmann Pseudopotential Methods for Porous Media Applications
summary: Pseudopotential models are a well established approach for multiphase and multicomponent simulations using the lattice Boltzmann method. Although not the most accurate, they are often chosen for ease of implementation and adaptability. A drawback of the models are spurious currents at the interfaces and particularly at solid walls which introduce numerical artifacts. An improved lattice Boltzmann pseudopotential model is presented. The discrete fluid density gradients in the coupling force are computed with rotationally symmetric gradient operators formulated as a convolution. As a result, spurious currents are reduced in settings where solid walls are unaligned with the lattice directions. Additionally, variations of introducing fluid-solid interaction either equally through both fluids or through a single fluid only are compared. Presented model variants are compared using droplets on walls as a common benchmark, analytically solvable capillary rise experiments (Jurin's law), and porous media imbibition as a practical application. Rotationally symmetric operators outperform the classical lattice weights approach in all tests in terms of accuracy, while avoiding extending the lattice to compute higher order gradients. The choice of the fluid-solid interaction variant depends on the problem under consideration and the desired properties of the resulting model.

title: Irreversible dynamics for ideal fluids on Riemannian manifolds: metriplectic energy-conserving alternatives to Navier-Stokes
comment: 32 pages, no figures, first version. All comments are welcome!
summary: For modelling dissipative phenomena such as friction, diffusion and viscosity, the Hamiltonian framework has a key limitation: once the Casimir invariants are fixed, Hamiltonian flows preserve phase-space volume, which rules out relaxation to equilibrium. Thus modelling dissipation requires modifying the Hamiltonian structure. Following the metriplectic (equivalently, GENERIC) approach, we add to the Hamiltonian vector field a dissipative term generated by a symmetric bracket, here constructed from a Riemannian metric. The resulting flow conserves the energy, and optionally further invariants, while driving a chosen generalised entropy monotonically, which makes the dynamics irreversible; when the entropy is bounded on energy level sets in the direction in which it is driven, it acts as a Lyapunov functional. We apply this construction to ideal fluids on compact Riemannian manifolds, choosing Casimirs of the Lie-Poisson bracket as entropies. In two dimensions, dissipating enstrophy yields the already-known energy-constrained Navier-Stokes equations, which include a nonlocal term restoring energy balance. In three dimensions, where enstrophy is no longer a Casimir, we derive new irreversible models. For incompressible and compressible fluids carrying an advected scalar, dissipating potential enstrophy or higher potential-vorticity moments gives a nonlinear, anisotropic diffusion that acts to align the gradients of the scalar and of the potential vorticity. For a purely incompressible fluid, taking helicity as the entropy gives a first-order, non-smoothing dissipative term whose stationary states are Beltrami fields.

title: An Invariant Neural-Network Eddy-Viscosity Closure with Iterative Solver Coupling for Molten Salt Fast Reactor Thermal-Hydraulics
comment: 42 pages, 12 figures
summary: System thermal-hydraulics codes such as the System Analysis Module (SAM) close turbulence on coarse meshes with algebraic zero-equation mixing-length models. These models cannot represent the non-equilibrium turbulence, flow separation, and large-scale recirculation of open-cavity advanced reactors. We develop an invariant neural-network eddy-viscosity closure for SAM and apply it to the Molten Salt Fast Reactor (MSFR). The closure predicts the turbulent kinetic energy and timescale of each element from the flow and geometry of its neighbors, without solving turbulence transport equations. The resulting non-negative eddy viscosity enters the implicit diffusive operator, which keeps the momentum equations well conditioned. We prove that the closure is exactly invariant to translation, Galilean boost, rotation, reflection, and neighbor ordering. A network trained on high-order Nek5000 fields sees a different feature distribution on the coarse SAM mesh. We remove this covariate shift by iteratively retraining the network on SAM flow states against fixed Nek5000 targets. For a held-out steady state, the coupled closure reproduces the single recirculation cell and eddy-viscosity plume of the Nek5000 reference. In a 120 s pump-coastdown transient, it halves the velocity error of the mixing-length model, from 37.6% to 17.7%, and matches the Nek5000 eddy viscosity with a time-averaged relative error of 12%. The remaining velocity error comes from the coarse mesh. The coupled transient takes about 0.2 core-hours, compared with about 330 core-hours for Nek5000. The results show that the closure can recover two-equation RANS turbulence behavior in a coarse-mesh system code at a small fraction of the CFD cost.

title: Spatiotemporal learning improves quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement
comment: 48 pages, 9 figures, 18 tables, including Supplementary Information
summary: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information. It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.

title: Stretched bilayer-cytoskeleton links hold echinocytes in a model splenic slit
comment: 35 pages, 8 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Materials included (pages S1-S16, 6 figures, 1 table); Movies S1 to S3 are ancillary files. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Stored red blood cells become echinocytes, growing spicules before losing membrane; the spleen clears the resulting small, spherical cells. Whether spicules alone hinder splenic passage is unknown. Shape and area change together. In a two-component model whose shrinking cytoskeleton raises spicules, we drove a discocyte and stage I to III echinocytes of equal area and volume through a model splenic slit. The pressure drop needed to pass rose with stage; stage III echinocytes were held at 37 to 50 times the pressure drop that passed the discocyte. Bilayer-cytoskeleton links stretched near full extension held these cells; lengthening them about twofold released a held cell. Capillary-sized channels, as in our device, separated the stages far less. Of the shape classes in stored blood, the model held at high pressure drops only storage-induced microerythrocytes, which perfused human spleens clear most. Spicules, besides membrane loss, may decide which stored cells the spleen retains.
